source: Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976) The role of tutoring in problem solving
finding: Introduced the word scaffolding. One adult tutor helped young children build a wooden pyramid from interlocking blocks. The paper lists tutor functions: recruit the child, cut the degrees of freedom, keep direction, mark critical features, control frustration, demonstrate. The child does the parts he can; the tutor takes the rest.
numbers: Secondary summaries only: 30 children, ages 3, 4 and 5 (10 per age), one tutor who was a paper author, 21 blocks. Not verified against the paper text.
quote: a scaffolding process that enables a child or novice to solve a problem, carry out a task or achieve a goal which would be beyond his unassisted efforts (as quoted in secondary sources, p. 90)
limits: Full text could not be fetched (publisher PDF blocked). Numbers come from search summaries and are unverified. No control group; the tutor was an author; results are descriptive, not tested.
agent_relevance: The first definition ties support to the learner's current gap and to a goal of hand-over. A scaffold that never hands back is not a scaffold. For us this means each hint our code gives should be tied to a named failing step and should be removable.

source: Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976) The role of tutoring in problem solving
finding: Later reviews describe three defining features: contingency (tutor checks what the learner can do and gives just enough), intersubjectivity, and transfer of responsibility (fade the support until the learner works alone).
numbers: Defining features as restated in the opened Belland et al. (2017) text, not read in the 1976 paper.
limits: Wood et al. 1976 itself mentions a wider range of change than only fading (adding support too), per Belland et al. Later work often narrowed scaffolding to fading.
agent_relevance: Three tests for any scaffold in our schema: is it sized to the observed failure, does it share the goal, is there a code-checked rule that removes it.

source: Smit, de Kleijn, Wicherts & van de Pol (2025) What it takes to tutor: a preregistered direct replication of the scaffolding experimental study by Wood et al. (1978)
finding: A preregistered direct replication of Wood, Wood and Middleton (1978), the main experiment that tested contingent tutoring. The original found contingent instruction beat three less contingent styles. The replication did not reproduce that effect on the children's independent performance after teaching.
numbers: N = 285 three-year-olds, randomly assigned to four conditions: demonstration, verbal instruction, swing (demonstration plus verbal), contingent instruction. Instruction times matched the original. Tutor accuracy 68.9% vs 70% in the original. Failed to replicate the contingent-instruction effect on later independent problem solving.
limits: Only the abstract-level page was read this session; Bayes factors and per-condition means not seen. A web summary says Bayes factors gave strong evidence for the null, which I could not confirm. Original sample size not seen.
agent_relevance: The best-known experimental support for contingent scaffolding did not replicate in the one direct test. So do not assume contingent hint sizing beats simple fixed help just because the theory says so. Test it on our own tasks.

source: Klahr & Nigam (2004) The equivalence of learning paths in early science instruction
finding: Direct instruction vs discovery in learning to design unconfounded experiments (control of variables). More children learned from direct instruction. But the children who learned from direct instruction later judged science-fair posters as well as the few who discovered the method alone (path independence).
numbers: N = 112 third- and fourth-grade children. Two points measured: acquisition of the control-of-variables procedure, then transfer to evaluating science-fair posters. Commonly quoted split is about 77% mastery under direct instruction vs 23% under discovery, but I did not see those figures in text I read.
limits: Only the abstract was read (via Europe PMC). The 77/23 split is from memory and secondary summaries and is unverified. One domain, one age band, one procedure.
agent_relevance: Gives the cleanest small-scale case that a strong scaffold wins for acquisition and costs nothing at transfer. Supports giving the agent explicit procedures for rare, hard moves instead of hoping it discovers them.

source: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work
finding: The central claim: for novices, minimally guided learning (discovery, problem-based, inquiry, experiential, constructivist teaching) is less effective and less efficient than fully guided teaching. Direct guidance is defined as fully explaining the concepts and procedures plus a learning strategy that fits human cognitive architecture. Learning is defined as a change in long-term memory.
numbers: Argument and literature review, no new data and no pooled effect size. The paper cites about 50 years of disputes (Ausubel 1964, Craig 1956, Mayer 2004).
quote: Controlled experiments almost uniformly indicate that when dealing with novel information, learners should be explicitly shown what to do and how to do it.
limits: The paper sets up a binary of fully guided vs minimal guidance. Its critics say the targeted methods are in fact scaffolded. It is selective in the studies it cites and gives no inclusion rules.
agent_relevance: Gives the default for novice-level slots: tell the model the procedure, do not ask it to rediscover it. Fits our rule that code decides and the model fills a slot.

source: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work
finding: Mechanism: working memory is small and short, long-term memory holds the schemas that make experts fast. Discovery makes novices search the problem space, which loads working memory and builds no schema. Evidence for the memory-based view comes from chess: experts recall real board positions far better than novices but not random positions (De Groot; Chase and Simon 1973), a result replicated in other fields.
numbers: No numbers given in this paper for the chess result; it cites De Groot (1945/1965), Chase and Simon (1973), Egan and Schwartz (1979), Jeffries et al. (1981), Sweller and Cooper (1985).
limits: This paper reports no direct measure of cognitive load. Chess recall is an indirect argument for novice guidance.
agent_relevance: A model's context window is its working memory. Heavy free search inside one prompt costs accuracy; split search into code-driven small steps.

source: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work
finding: The worked-example effect is the paper's strongest evidence: novices who study worked examples beat novices who solve the same problems. Boundary conditions: it does not appear if the examples themselves carry a heavy load (Tarmizi and Sweller 1988; Ward and Sweller 1990). It first disappears and then reverses as expertise rises (Kalyuga et al. 2001, 2003). So guidance can be relaxed only as long-term memory takes over.
numbers: No pooled effect size in this paper; it cites many replications of the effect. Worked-example work is covered in subfield 01 and expertise reversal in 02; do not duplicate.
limits: The reversal point is the exact place where the paper itself says to withdraw support. That is why 'fully guided' is not a fixed prescription.
agent_relevance: Our fading rule has a theory behind it: remove a hint class after the agent has solved that class several times without it, and check the held-out cases (G3).

source: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work
finding: Tuovinen and Sweller (1999) compared exploration practice (a discovery technique) with worked examples. Exploration produced a much larger cognitive load and poorer learning for low-knowledge learners. High-knowledge learners were not hurt and benefited equally from both.
numbers: Numbers not given in Kirschner et al.; the primary Tuovinen and Sweller paper was not opened.
limits: Second-hand description of a single study. The interaction with prior knowledge is the point.
agent_relevance: Same hint, different value by competence. Our scaffold schedule needs a competence signal (past pass rate in code), not a fixed script.

source: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work
finding: The scaffolding effect appears as an aptitude-treatment interaction. Cronbach and Snow's (1977) review found replicated interactions: strong treatments help less able learners, weak treatments help more able ones. The paper says this anticipated the now recognised scaffolding effect.
numbers: Quote from Kyllonen and Lajoie (2003, p. 82). No effect sizes in Kirschner et al.
quote: strong treatments benefited less able learners and weaker treatments benefited more able learners
limits: Aptitude-treatment interaction findings have a poor replication record in general; the paper treats them as support without discussing that.
agent_relevance: Two agent arms may be needed: guided for weak starting states, light for strong ones. Choose the arm in code from an early probe.

source: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work
finding: Problem-based learning (PBL) evidence in medicine is used as a test case. Albanese and Mitchell (1993) meta-analysis: lower basic-science exam scores, no difference in residency selection, longer study hours; better clinical scores but more unnecessary tests, possibly from more clinical time. Berkson (1993) did not replicate the clinical advantage. Colliver (2000) found no statistical effect on educational outcomes in PBL studies.
numbers: No pooled numbers in the paper. Mixed evidence: some outcomes favour PBL.
limits: PBL curricula are not minimal guidance; later authors argue this is a category error. The paper picks outcomes that favour its case.
agent_relevance: Warning against reading 'structured but open' regimes as proof against support. Judge by outcome per item, not by label.

source: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work
finding: Mayer (2004) reviewed 50 years of studies comparing pure discovery with guided teaching and found that each decade the unguided approach was rebranded and the evidence again favoured guidance. The paper also notes that teachers using constructivist methods end up adding scaffolding (Aulls 2002, case study of classroom practice).
numbers: Quote from Mayer (2004, p. 18) as cited. Review covers roughly 1950 to the late 1980s. Aulls (2002) is a qualitative case study, not a controlled test.
quote: the debate about discovery has been replayed many times in education but each time, the evidence has favored a guided approach to learning
limits: Mayer's review covered pure discovery, not scaffolded inquiry. The paper stretches the conclusion to PBL and inquiry teaching.
agent_relevance: Even when the stated method is open-ended, effective practice quietly carries scaffolds. Our loop should make its scaffolds explicit and countable.

source: Hmelo-Silver, Duncan & Chinn (2007) Scaffolding and achievement in problem-based and inquiry learning: a response to Kirschner, Sweller & Clark
finding: The main reply to Kirschner et al.: problem-based and inquiry learning are heavily scaffolded designs, so the 2006 paper attacked minimal guidance that those methods do not use. Cited in the opened Alfieri et al. (2011) as a statement that constructivism does not claim all learning should be unaided.
numbers: Not given; source was not opened. Claim taken from the citation in Alfieri et al. (2011).
limits: Pointer only. Needs an opened copy before any detail is relied on.
agent_relevance: The dispute is really about what counts as guidance. Define our scaffolds operationally (what the code supplies and when) to avoid the same ambiguity.

source: Clark, Kirschner & Sweller (2012) Putting students on the path to learning: the case for fully guided instruction
finding: Plain-language version of the 2006 case. It adds a point on the achievement gap: in a review of about 70 studies (Clark 1989), skilled learners learned more with less guidance, less-skilled learners learned more with more guidance. Some weak students given low guidance scored lower on post-test than pre-test.
numbers: About 70 studies in the Clark (1989) review; no effect sizes in the article. The article says guidance should be faded out as knowledge and skill increase.
limits: A magazine-style article; the 70-study review is old (1989) and was not opened.
agent_relevance: Backs a rule that the same agent should get more guidance on the tasks where it starts weak, and that too little guidance can leave it worse than a plain baseline.

source: Clark, Kirschner & Sweller (2012) Putting students on the path to learning: the case for fully guided instruction
finding: A companion piece by Rosenshine in the same issue reports teacher success rates: in a fourth-grade math study 82% of answers were correct in the best teachers' classrooms vs 73% in the least successful. It says the optimal success rate during practice is about 80%.
numbers: 82% vs 73%; about 80% as the optimal practice success rate. Single cited study.
limits: Read as a teaching-practice heuristic, not as a laboratory result; no experiment tested 80% as a causal target.
agent_relevance: A usable fading trigger: withdraw hints once the agent passes about four of five checks on a class of subproblem; restore them if it drops.

source: Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich & Tenenbaum (2011) Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning?
finding: Meta-analysis 1: unassisted discovery (no guidance, no feedback) vs explicit instruction. Explicit instruction was better.
numbers: 108 studies, 580 comparisons. Mean d = -0.38 (95% CI -0.50 to -0.25), random effects; heterogeneity Q(107) = 522.11, p < .001.
limits: Heavy heterogeneity. Publication tier mattered: first-tier journals d = -0.67, second-tier -0.24, book chapters -0.12 and unpublished -0.01 (the last two not significant).
agent_relevance: Unassisted exploration inside one prompt should be the rare case, and anything exploratory should be given feedback from a check.

source: Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich & Tenenbaum (2011) Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning?
finding: Where unassisted discovery lost by domain and by age, and which explicit comparison it lost to. The worst comparison was against worked examples.
numbers: By domain: math d = -0.16, science -0.39, problem solving -0.48, verbal and social skills -0.95. By age: adolescents -0.53 vs adults -0.26. By comparison: direct teaching -0.29, feedback -0.46, worked examples -0.63, explanations provided -0.28. Acquisition scores -0.95, post-test -0.35, time to solution -0.21.
limits: Post hoc tests showed the worked-example contrast was larger than the direct-teaching contrast. Domain labels were set by the authors and the cells differ a lot in size.
agent_relevance: Rank of help types, in order of how much they beat doing nothing: worked example > feedback > direct teaching. Suggests a hint menu for the agent: show a solved example first, give check feedback second, plain statement of the rule third.

source: Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich & Tenenbaum (2011) Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning?
finding: Meta-analysis 2: enhanced discovery (guided discovery with scaffolding or feedback, elicited self-explanation, generation) vs other teaching. Enhanced discovery did better. The authors read this as support for scaffolded tasks and explanation prompts with feedback.
numbers: 56 studies, 360 comparisons. Mean d = 0.30 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.44); Q(55) = 260.14, p < .001. Dropping the 24 physical/motor comparisons: d = 0.25. Adults gained more than children; adolescents least.
limits: Generation conditions (make the learner produce answers with little else) did not beat other teaching. Unpublished studies and dissertations showed d = -0.54 against enhanced discovery, though four of five were generation designs. Highly heterogeneous.
agent_relevance: Asking the model to produce more (generate) does not help by itself; supplying a structure plus check feedback does. This lines up with our G2 (revise only from real output).

source: Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich & Tenenbaum (2011) Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning?
finding: The authors concluded that effective practice has at least one of: scaffolding in place, explanation tasks with timely accurate feedback, or worked examples. They also wrote that learners need to be redirected when they mis-construct.
numbers: Stated in the discussion; derived from the two meta-analyses above, not a third test.
limits: Recommendations are the authors' reading; no direct test of a combined scaffold. Only the initial-learning side, with little on how scaffolds were removed.
agent_relevance: Direct source for 'redirect on error' as the active ingredient, which is something our code can do from a failing check.

source: Belland, Walker, Kim & Lefler (2017) Synthesizing results from empirical research on computer-based scaffolding in STEM education
finding: Meta-analysis of computer-based scaffolding in STEM problem-centred teaching, primary school to adults. Scaffolding helped on average, and across contexts.
numbers: 144 studies, 333 outcomes (after averaging 515 to 333); Hedges g = 0.46 overall. Egger test for publication bias: p = .166. Five outliers from 3 studies were removed; four of five compared scaffolded learners with controls given complex problem solving with no support at all.
limits: Search window January 1993 to December 2014. Only STEM and computer-based scaffolds. Control groups received some intervention without scaffolding.
agent_relevance: A solid average for tool-delivered hints: about half a standard deviation. A plausible upper reference for what a scaffold layer might buy on our tasks.

source: Belland, Walker, Kim & Lefler (2017) Synthesizing results from empirical research on computer-based scaffolding in STEM education
finding: The test of the core scaffolding idea. Effect sizes did not differ among scaffolds that faded, added support, did both, or did neither. They also did not differ by the logic used to customise (performance-based, self-selected, fixed) or by whether the scaffold was context-specific. The effect was strongest in adults, far from the preschoolers of the original theory.
numbers: No moderator difference found on fading/adding/fading-adding/none. The authors cite a 2015 meta-analysis (Belland, Walker, Olsen and Leary) where scaffolds NOT faded on a fixed schedule did better than faded ones.
limits: Absence of a difference is not proof of equality; power per subgroup may be low (subgroup sizes not extracted).
agent_relevance: Withdrawal is not shown to matter in the aggregate, and a fixed-timer fade may hurt. If we fade at all, do it on measured pass rate, and treat fading as a hypothesis to test per task type.

source: Belland, Walker & Kim (2017) A Bayesian network meta-analysis to synthesize the influence of contexts of scaffolding use on cognitive outcomes in STEM education
finding: Companion analysis of pre-post (within-subject) gains from scaffolding. It also reports that earlier between-group meta-analyses gave 0.53 and 0.46 SD for scaffolding over control.
numbers: 56 studies, 20,000 MCMC samples. Effects strong across subgroups. For students with learning disabilities, g = 3.13 (very large).
limits: Within-subject pre-post gains are inflated by repeated testing and are not comparable with control-group effect sizes. The 3.13 figure is from a small subgroup.
agent_relevance: Do not compare pre-post lift with controlled lift. Our scaffold evaluation must use a no-scaffold control on held-out items.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning in large language models
finding: Least-to-most prompting is a coded scaffold: first split the problem into easier subproblems, then solve them in order, each helped by earlier answers. It beat chain-of-thought when test problems were harder than the examples.
numbers: SCAN length split with code-davinci-002: standard 16.7%, chain-of-thought 16.2%, least-to-most 99.7% (14 mapping exemplars + 8 decomposition exemplars). text-davinci-002 76.0% (100-command subset); code-davinci-001 60.7%. Only 13 failures on the full length-split test set.
limits: Decomposition is taken as easy on SCAN. The authors say decomposition prompts do not generalise across problem types, even inside one domain. A model-chosen decomposition, not a human-written one, is used at test time.
agent_relevance: The closest LLM analogue of support-then-answer: the program feeds each subproblem and the previous answer. Strong evidence that a scaffold the code controls moves a model past its examples.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning in large language models
finding: Length generalisation in last-letter concatenation: the gap between scaffolded and unscaffolded grows with difficulty.
numbers: Least-to-most vs chain-of-thought accuracy (code-davinci-002, 500 lists per length): L=4 94.0 vs 84.2; L=6 88.4 vs 69.2; L=8 83.0 vs 50.2; L=10 76.4 vs 39.8; L=12 74.0 vs 31.8. Standard prompting 0.0 at every length. With 4 or 8 independent chain-of-thought exemplars at L=12: 37.4% and 38.4%, still well below 74.0%.
limits: One synthetic task, one model family (GPT-3 code-davinci-002). Prompts for least-to-most are longer, a confound the authors partly address with extra chain-of-thought exemplars.
agent_relevance: Scaffold benefit scales with how far the test is from the examples. The same would be expected for harder items in our benchmarks.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning in large language models
finding: On math word problems the scaffold gave small gains overall and larger gains on long problems. Almost every GSM8K failure was solvable with a hand-made decomposition.
numbers: GSM8K: chain-of-thought 60.87% vs least-to-most 62.39% overall; problems needing at least 5 steps: 39.07% vs 45.23%. DROP numeric subset: non-football 74.77 vs 82.45; football 59.56 vs 73.42.
limits: The model-produced decomposition is the weak link: if it picks the wrong sub-steps, the scaffold fails. Gain is only 1.5 points on all of GSM8K.
agent_relevance: A scaffold is only as good as its plan step. Plan quality should be checked in code, for example by verifying sub-answers, before more guidance is added.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: evidence from high school mathematics
finding: Field RCT with GPT-4 tutors in high-school maths. Plain ChatGPT-style access raised practice scores but lowered later unaided exam scores. A tutor whose prompt gave hints without final answers, with teacher-provided solutions, removed most of the harm.
numbers: Turkey, Fall 2023-24, about 50 classes, nearly 1,000 students in grades 9-11, four 90-minute sessions. Practice (assisted): GPT Base +0.137 (SE 0.031), GPT Tutor +0.361 (SE 0.032) vs control mean 0.284, i.e. +48% and +127%. Exam (unassisted): GPT Base -0.054 (SE 0.022), about -17% vs control mean 0.321; GPT Tutor -0.004 (SE 0.013), not significant.
limits: Only maths, one school, short horizon (exam in the same session). GPT Tutor did not beat the control on the exam, so the scaffold prevented harm but did not add learning.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of 'support without withdrawal'. Help that leaves no work for the learner raises assisted performance and lowers unassisted skill. For our agent, a scaffold that supplies answers will pass in-loop checks and then fail on the held-out check.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: evidence from high school mathematics
finding: Mechanism and self-awareness in the same study. Students used GPT Base as a crutch, asking for and copying solutions, but used GPT Tutor to ask for help or try answers themselves. Students did not see the harm.
numbers: GPT Base students did worse on the exam but did not report learning less. GPT Tutor students did not score better on the exam but reported performing significantly better. The paper also examines how the error rate in GPT Base solutions on assisted problems affects later exam performance (details not extracted).
limits: Self-report in a classroom; perception measures are noisy. Mismatch between perceived and actual learning is also reported in other settings.
agent_relevance: Self-assessed progress is not evidence of skill. Pairs with guardrail G2 and G3: a pass needs to be on unassisted held-out items.

source: Kestin et al. (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning
finding: Randomised crossover at Harvard: a custom GPT-4 tutor following active-learning practice beat an in-class active-learning lesson on the same physics content, in less time. The designers wrote that a system prompt alone could not reliably scaffold multi-part problems, so the platform walks students through each part in sequence.
numbers: N = 194 undergraduates. Median post-test 4.5 (AI group) vs 3.5 (in-class). Linear-regression effect 0.63 SD; quantile regression estimate 0.73 to 1.3 SD. Median time on task 49 min (AI group) vs 60 min lesson. 83% of students rated the tutor's explanations as good as or better than the instructor's. Prompts were enriched with step-by-step solutions to limit errors.
limits: One course, crossover design; post-test ceiling effect acknowledged by the authors. A post-test shortly after the lesson was the outcome; no retention test seen. 30% of AI-group students spent over 60 minutes.
agent_relevance: Scaffolding order by code, not by the model, was needed to keep the tutor on track; the same split we use (program sequences, model fills slots).

source: Lehmann, Cornelius & Sting (2025) AI meets the classroom: when do large language models harm learning?
finding: Two preregistered lab experiments plus a field study on programming. LLM access had no effect on overall learning. The effect depended on use: substituting for practice (asking for solutions) raised how much was covered but cut understanding; complementing practice (asking for explanations) raised understanding. LLM help widened the gap by prior knowledge.
numbers: Study 2: 108 recruited, 107 analysed (79% no prior Python); Study 3: 72 enrolled, 69 analysed. Treated subjects sent on average 4.45 messages to the LLM in Study 2. In Study 3, copy-and-paste lowered topic understanding. Field study: two graduate programming courses in a Dutch university; exogenous variation in LLM availability gave a significant long-term decline in outcomes.
limits: Small lab samples, 45-minute learning phase, novice Python. Usage-type effects are exploratory, not preregistered.
agent_relevance: Matches the 'support then withdrawal' logic: the type of help decides the outcome. Also: weak starters were harmed by LLM help and strong starters helped, which echoes expertise reversal in reverse.

source: Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb & Demszky (2024/2026) Tutor CoPilot: a human-AI approach for scaling real-time expertise
finding: RCT where an LLM wrote real-time suggestions based on expert tutors' thinking, shown to human tutors in live maths tutoring. Students of tutors with access mastered more topics, most for weaker tutors.
numbers: Intent-to-treat: +4 percentage points exit-ticket pass rate (62% to 66%, p < .01). Up to +9 points for students of lower-rated or less experienced tutors. Treatment-on-treated: 62% to 76% (+14). 900 tutors initially assigned (450 per arm), 783 in the analysis; more than 1,000 students; annual cost about $20 per tutor. Participation points and student survey outcomes: no significant effect, though preregistered.
limits: Effects shrink as tutor skill rises (a hint of expertise reversal). One provider, one district, one 2-month window. In one subgroup analysis, less experienced treated tutors used generic encouragement less but did not adopt more of the other measured strategies.
agent_relevance: A scaffold for the helper, not the learner. The weakest performers gained most, so first deploy scaffolds where the baseline is weakest, and expect little for strong runs.

source: Macina et al. (2023) MathDial: a dialogue tutoring dataset with rich pedagogical properties
finding: A dialogue dataset of teachers scaffolding sixth-grade maths errors, with a move taxonomy built on Reiser (2004): structuring moves (Focus) and problematizing moves (Probing), plus Telling. LLM tutors tend to reveal the answer too soon.
numbers: Teachers resolved confusion in about 89% of dialogues, about 75% mostly by scaffolding questions and about 14% by revealing most of the answer. Focus questions were 37% of utterances. Telling rose as dialogues went on. Interactive tutoring with an LLM student: Success@5 / Telling@5 = NextStep 25% / 0%, ChatGPT 29% / 16%, Flan-T5 (780M, fine-tuned) 30% / under 1%, human ground truth 59% / under 1%. At 10 turns: ChatGPT 53% / 32%; Flan-T5 39% / 4%; ground truth 82% / 4%.
limits: Student was an LLM (InstructGPT), a teacher panel judged it plausible; the paper's own metric, not a learning outcome with humans. Resolutions judged by the teachers themselves.
agent_relevance: Shows a tradeoff the agent will face: more telling gives higher solve rate but defeats the point. Our scaffold should count telling moves in code and cap them.

source: LearnLM Team, Google (2024) LearnLM: improving Gemini for learning
finding: Google's LearnLM recasts tutoring as pedagogical instruction following: system prompts say what pedagogy is wanted, such as 'do not give away the answer', and the model is trained to obey even when a learner pushes back. Expert raters preferred it over contemporaneous models.
numbers: Average preference strength for LearnLM: 31% over GPT-4o, 11% over Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 13% over Gemini 1.5 Pro (expert raters role-playing learners in scripted scenarios; 1,024 written explanations collected; 203 sampled for themes). Explanations favouring LearnLM were more likely to mention keeps_on_topic, challenges_learner and gives_away_answers (probably as a complaint about other models; context not checked).
limits: Judged by experts role-playing learners, not by real learning outcomes. Vendor evaluation. Data comes from short scripted sessions.
agent_relevance: Evidence that holding back the answer is a trained behavior that default models lack, and that prompt-level instructions are the lever for developers. The same holds for our slots: encode the withhold rule in code, not as a polite request.
